intro: We use the **past simple** for finished actions and situations in the past: *I visited my grandmother yesterday.* Regular verbs add **-ed** (*work → worked*). Irregular verbs have their own past form (*go → went*).
In negatives and questions, we use **did** + the base verb: *I didn't go. Did you go?*

sections.h2: When do we use the past simple?

items: A finished action at a finished time: *She **called** me last night.*
Actions one after another: *He **got up**, **had** a shower and **left** for work.*
A situation or habit that was true in the past but is finished now: *We **lived** in Toronto for five years.* (We don't live there now.)
Stories: *A young girl **found** an old key in the garden.*

blocks.md: Common time words: *yesterday, last night, last week, last year, two days ago, in 2019, when I was a child.*

sections.h2: How to form the past simple

rows: I **didn't work** late. She **didn't go** home.
Yes, + subject + did. / No, + subject + didn't.
Yes, I did. / No, she didn't.

blocks.md: The past form is the same for every person: *I, you, he, she, it, we, they **worked***. There is no -s in the past.
**Be** is different. Use **was** (I, he, she, it) and **were** (you, we, they), and don't use did: *I **wasn't** tired. **Were** you at home?*

rows: work → worked, watch → watched, clean → cleaned
live → lived, like → liked, dance → danced
study → studied, try → tried, carry → carried
play → played, enjoy → enjoyed, stay → stayed
One vowel + one consonant at the end of a stressed syllable: double the consonant
stop → stopped, plan → planned, prefer → preferred

blocks.md: We don't double the consonant when the last syllable is not stressed: *visit → visited, open → opened, listen → listened.*
British and American spelling are different for some verbs ending in **-l**: *travel → travelled* (UK) / *traveled* (US), *cancel → cancelled* (UK) / *canceled* (US). Both are correct.

rows: stopped, worked, kissed, washed, watched, laughed
after vowel sounds and the sounds /b/, /g/, /v/, /z/, /l/, /m/, /n/

blocks.md: -ed only adds an extra syllable after a **t** or **d** sound. *Worked* and *played* have one syllable; *wan-ted* has two.

Irregular verbs don't use -ed, so you need to learn their past forms. The third column is the past participle, which you need for the present perfect (*I have **seen***) and the passive (*It was **made***).

Use the past simple when you say or know **when** it happened: *I **lost** my keys yesterday.* Use the present perfect when the time isn't important and the result matters now: *I**'ve lost** my keys.* (I can't find them now.) More practice: [Present Perfect vs Past Simple](/blog/grammar/present-perfect-vs-past-simple/).

items.text: I **watched** a film last night.
We **went** to the beach on Saturday.
She **didn't call** me yesterday.
**Did** you **finish** your homework?
They **moved** to Canada in 2018.
He **was** very tired after work.
**Were** the shops open on Sunday?
I **bought** a new phone two weeks ago.
When **did** the film **start**?
My grandfather **worked** in a bank for 30 years.
items.note: finished situation: he doesn't work there now

mistakes.wrong: Did you went to the party?
mistakes.right: Did you go to the party?
mistakes.why: After did, use the base verb.
After didn't, use the base verb.

mistakes.wrong: I was go to the park yesterday.
mistakes.right: I went to the park yesterday.
mistakes.why: Don't put was before a normal verb.
With be, use was/were, not did.
With a finished time like yesterday, use the past simple.

items.prompt: We ___ dinner at a Thai restaurant last night.
items.explanation: *Last night* is a finished time, so use the past simple. *Have* is irregular: have → **had**.

items.prompt: She ___ her keys this morning, so she couldn't open the door.
items.explanation: The action is finished, so use the past simple. *Lose* is irregular: lose → **lost**.

items.prompt: I ___ the email because I was busy.
items.explanation: Negative: **didn't** + base verb. Don't add -ed after didn't.

items.prompt: ___ you see the match last Sunday?
items.explanation: Questions: **Did** + subject + base verb. *Last Sunday* is a finished time.

items.prompt: They ___ to Spain two years ago.
items.explanation: *Two years ago* is a finished time. *Go* is irregular: go → **went**. (*Gone* needs *have*: *have gone*.)

items.prompt: My parents ___ at home when I arrived.
He ___ to the party because he was ill.
Where ___ you go on holiday last summer?
items.explanation: Wh- questions with a normal verb: question word + **did** + subject + base verb.

items.prompt: The children ___ in the garden all afternoon.
I ___ for my exam all weekend.
items.explanation: Consonant + y: change y to **-ied**: study → **studied**.

items.prompt: The bus ___ suddenly, and everyone fell forward.
items.explanation: *Stop* ends in one vowel + one consonant, so double the p: **stopped**.

items.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
items.explanation: After **didn't**, use the base verb: *didn't know*.

items.prompt: How much ___ your new laptop cost when you bought it?
items.explanation: *When you bought it* is in the past, so use **did** + base verb. *Cost* is irregular: cost → cost → cost.

items.prompt: ___ it cold in Montreal last week?
Last year, I ___ my first marathon.
items.explanation: *Last year* is a finished time, so use the past simple: run → **ran**.

items.prompt: Which verb has an extra syllable when you say the -ed ending?
items.explanation: *Want* ends in a t sound, so -ed sounds like /ɪd/ and adds a syllable: **want-ed**. The other three have one syllable.

intro: We use the **past continuous** for an action that was in progress at a time in the past: *At 8 o'clock last night, I **was watching** a film.* Form it with **was / were + verb-ing**.

We often use it together with the past simple. The past continuous is the longer background action; the past simple is the shorter action that happened in the middle of it: *I **was cooking** when the phone **rang**.*

sections.h2: How to form the past continuous

rows: Yes, + subject + was/were. / No, + subject + wasn't/weren't.
Yes, I was. / No, they weren't.

blocks.md: Use **was** with I, he, she, it and **were** with you, we, they.

sections.h2: When do we use the past continuous?

items: An action in progress at a time in the past: *At 10 p.m., we **were having** dinner.*
A longer action interrupted by a shorter one (past simple): *I **was walking** home when it **started** to rain.*
Two actions in progress at the same time: *While I **was studying**, my sister **was watching** TV.*
The background of a story: *The sun **was shining** and the birds **were singing**.*

blocks.md: We often use **when** before the short action (past simple) and **while** before the long action (past continuous):

items.text: I **was having** a shower **when** the doorbell **rang**.
**While** I **was having** a shower, the doorbell **rang**.

blocks.md: Compare: *When the phone rang, I **answered** it.* (first the phone rang, then I answered: past simple + past simple) and *When the phone rang, I **was cooking**.* (I was already cooking).

rows: an action in progress, not finished at that moment
*I **wrote** an email at 9.* (I wrote it at 9)
*I **was writing** an email at 9.* (I was in the middle of it)
*It **was raining** when I left the house.*

blocks.md: State verbs like *know, want, like, need* and *have* (= own) don't usually go in the continuous: *I **knew** the answer.* (not *I was knowing*)

items.text: At 7 o'clock this morning, I **was having** breakfast.
They **were playing** football when it **started** to snow.
**Were** you **sleeping** when I called?
She **wasn't wearing** a coat, so she was cold.
While we **were waiting** for the bus, we **saw** an accident.
What **were** you **doing** at midnight?
He **was driving** too fast when the police **stopped** him.
I **was reading** while my brother **was cooking**.
items.note: two actions at the same time

items.text: The children **were laughing** and the music **was playing**.
I **cut** my finger while I **was cooking**.

mistakes.wrong: I was work when you called.
mistakes.right: I was working when you called.

mistakes.why: Know is a state verb: use the past simple.

mistakes.wrong: I was walking home when I was seeing my teacher.
mistakes.right: I was walking home when I saw my teacher.
mistakes.why: The short action is past simple.
Past continuous questions use was/were, not did.

mistakes.wrong: She didn't sleeping when I got home.
mistakes.right: She wasn't sleeping when I got home.

items.prompt: At 9 p.m. yesterday, I ___ TV.
items.explanation: An action in progress at a past time: *I* + **was** + verb-ing.

items.prompt: They ___ football when it started to rain.
I was cooking when the phone ___.
items.explanation: The short action that interrupted: past simple. *Ring* → **rang**.

items.prompt: ___ you sleeping when I called?
items.explanation: Past continuous question with *you*: **Were** + subject + verb-ing.

items.prompt: While she ___ for the bus, she met an old friend.
What ___ you doing at midnight last night?
He ___ the answer, so he put his hand up.
items.explanation: *Know* is a state verb: past simple, **knew**.

items.prompt: I ___ my finger while I was cutting vegetables.
items.explanation: The short, sudden action: past simple. *Cut* → **cut**.

items.prompt: The sun ___ and the birds were singing.
items.explanation: Background of a story: *the sun* (it) + **was shining**.

items.prompt: We ___ when you rang the doorbell.
Choose the correct sentence.
options: I walked home when I was seeing my teacher.
I was walking home when I saw my teacher.
I was walk home when I saw my teacher.
I was walking home when I was see my teacher.

items.prompt: ___ the children playing outside when the storm started?
When I arrived at the party, my friends ___. (They started before I arrived.)
items.explanation: They were already in the middle of dancing: **were dancing**.

items.prompt: While I was studying, my brother ___ video games.
items.explanation: Two actions at the same time: *my brother* (he) + **was playing**.

items.prompt: It ___ when we left the house, so we took umbrellas.
items.explanation: The rain was in progress when we left: **was raining**.

items.prompt: When the bell rang, the students ___ their books and left.
items.explanation: One action after another: past simple, **closed** … and left.

intro: We use a **comparative** to compare two things: *My brother is **taller than** me.* We use a **superlative** to say one thing is more than all the others in a group: *He's **the tallest** person in our family.*
Short adjectives add **-er / -est** (*cheap, cheaper, the cheapest*). Longer adjectives use **more / the most** (*more expensive, the most expensive*).

sections.h2: How to form comparatives and superlatives

blocks.md: More examples of doubling: *hot → hotter, thin → thinner, sad → sadder, wet → wetter.* We don't double **w**: *new → newer, slow → slower.*
Some two-syllable adjectives can use both forms: *quiet → quieter / more quiet, simple → simpler / more simple, clever → cleverer / more clever.* Both are correct; the -er form is more common.
*Well* (= healthy) also becomes **better**: *I was ill last week, but I feel **better** now.*

sections.h2: How to use them in a sentence

items: Comparative + **than**: *Trains are **faster than** buses.*

**the** + superlative: *It's **the oldest** building in the city.* Use **in** with places and groups (*in the world, in my class*) and **of** with time periods and numbers (*of the year, of the three*).
Superlative + present perfect + **ever**: *It's **the best** film I've **ever** seen.*
**less / the least** is the opposite of more / the most: *This phone is **less expensive than** that one.*
**as … as** = the same; **not as … as** = less: *My sister is **as tall as** me. The second film **wasn't as good as** the first.*

blocks.md: To make a comparative stronger, use **much**, **a lot** or **far**: *much cheaper, a lot more expensive, far better.* Don't use *very* with comparatives.

items.text: My new flat is **bigger than** my old one.
This is **the most beautiful** beach I've ever seen.
Today is **hotter than** yesterday.
She's **the best** student in our class.
English is **easier** for me **than** French.
My laptop is **more expensive than** yours, but it's **slower**.
That was **the worst** meal of my life.
The bus is **cheaper than** the train, but it's **less comfortable**.
My brother isn't **as tall as** my sister.
The Nile is one of **the longest** rivers in the world.
items.note: one of the + superlative + plural noun

mistakes.wrong: She is more tall than me.

mistakes.why: Better is already a comparative. Don't add more.

mistakes.wrong: He is the most happiest person I know.
mistakes.right: He is the happiest person I know.

mistakes.wrong: My car is bigger then yours.
mistakes.right: My car is bigger than yours.

mistakes.wrong: It's the biggest city of the world.
mistakes.right: It's the biggest city in the world.

mistakes.why: Use much, a lot or far with comparatives, not very.
Bad is irregular: bad → worse → the worst.

items.prompt: My bag is ___ than yours.
items.explanation: *Heavy* ends in consonant + y: y → **-ier**. Use the comparative with *than*.

items.prompt: Everest is ___ mountain in the world.
items.explanation: We compare one mountain with all the others, so use the superlative: **the highest**.

items.prompt: This is ___ restaurant in town.
Flying is ___ than driving, but it's more expensive.
This exam was ___ than the last one. I failed it!
My new job is ___ than my old one.
I feel ___ today than yesterday. My cold has almost gone.
Yesterday was ___ day of the year so far.
items.explanation: *Hot* ends in one vowel + one consonant, so double the t: **the hottest**.

items.prompt: This sofa is ___ comfortable than the old one.
items.explanation: Make a comparative stronger with **much**: *much more comfortable*. Don't use *very*.

items.prompt: Your phone is ___ mine.
items.explanation: *New* → newer (we don't double w). Use **than**, not then.

items.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: She's the intelligentest student in the class.
She's the most intelligent student in the class.
She's more intelligent student in the class.
She's most intelligent than the class.

items.prompt: The film wasn't ___ the book.
Is London ___ Paris?
Neptune is ___ planet from the sun.
items.explanation: *Far* is irregular: far → further/farther → **the furthest**/the farthest.

items.prompt: It was ___ film I've ever seen.
items.explanation: Superlative + *I've ever*: funny → **the funniest**. Don't use most and -est together.

items.prompt: Train tickets are ___ than plane tickets.
items.explanation: **Less** + adjective + than is the opposite of *more … than*.

topics.h1: Future Forms: Going To, Will and Present Continuous
intro: English has several ways to talk about the future. The three most common are **be going to** (plans and predictions from evidence), **will** (decisions, offers, promises and opinions) and the **present continuous** (arranged plans).
Often more than one form is possible. The guide below shows the usual choice in each situation.

sections.h2: Be going to: plans and evidence

blocks.md: Form: **am / is / are + going to + base verb**. Negative: *She **isn't going to** come.* Question: ***Are** you **going to** buy it?*

items: A plan or intention you decided before now: *I**'m going to** visit my aunt this weekend.*
A prediction based on what you can see now: *Look at those clouds. It**'s going to** rain.*

sections.h2: Will: decisions, offers, promises and opinions

blocks.md: Form: **will / 'll + base verb**. Negative: **won't** (will not).

items: A decision made at the moment of speaking: *I'm thirsty. I**'ll** get some water.*
Offers: *That bag looks heavy. I**'ll** carry it.*
Promises: *I **won't** be late, I promise.*
Predictions based on your opinion: *I think you**'ll** love this film.*

blocks.md: For offers and suggestions with *I* and *we*, use **shall** in questions: ***Shall** I help you? **Shall** we go?* In American English, *Should I…?* is also common.
Use the present continuous for future plans that are fixed, usually with a time and other people involved: *I**'m meeting** Sam at 6 tonight. We**'re flying** to Rome on Monday.*
*Be going to* is also correct here: *I'm going to meet Sam at 6.* The present continuous just sounds more fixed. Timetables and schedules often use the present simple: *The film **starts** at 8.*

rows: an arrangement with a time or place
*I'll help you. Shall I call a taxi?*
*I think it'll be a great party.*

blocks.md: Don't use the present simple for decisions, offers or promises: *I**'ll** answer it.* (not *I answer it*)

items.text: We**'re going to** paint the kitchen this weekend.
Look out! That glass **is going to** fall.
I'm tired. I think I**'ll** go to bed.
I**'ll** call you tomorrow, I promise.
**Shall** I make some tea?
She**'s starting** her new job on Monday.
I don't think it**'ll** rain tomorrow.
**Are** you **going to** watch the match tonight?
They **aren't coming** to the party. They're busy.
The concert **starts** at 8 p.m.

mistakes.wrong: The phone's ringing. I answer it.
mistakes.right: The phone's ringing. I'll answer it.

mistakes.wrong: I promise I don't tell anyone.
mistakes.right: I promise I won't tell anyone.

mistakes.wrong: I think it is raining tomorrow.
mistakes.right: I think it will rain tomorrow.

items.prompt: I ___ visit my grandparents this weekend. I bought the train tickets yesterday.
items.explanation: A plan made before now: **am going to** + base verb.

items.prompt: A: We've run out of milk. B: Oh, really? I ___ some on my way home.
items.explanation: B decides now: **'ll buy** (will + base verb).

items.prompt: It's cold in here. ___ I close the window?
She ___ study medicine at university.
items.explanation: A plan: **is going to** + base verb.

items.prompt: Don't worry, I ___ tell anyone. I promise.
A: Tea or coffee? B: I ___ coffee, please.
items.explanation: A decision at the moment of speaking: **'ll have**.

items.prompt: Look at those black clouds! It ___ rain.
items.explanation: A prediction from evidence you can see: **is going to**.

items.prompt: We ___ dinner with Tom and Anna at 7 tonight. We booked the table last week.
items.explanation: A fixed arrangement: present continuous, **are having**.

items.prompt: ___ you going to watch the match tonight?
Which sentence is a promise?
options: I'm going to the gym on Monday.
items.explanation: Promises use **will**: *I'll always love you.* The others are a plan, a prediction and a timetable.

items.prompt: Be careful! You ___ fall!
items.explanation: A prediction from what we can see now: **are going to**.

items.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
They ___ to the party. They have to work.
I think you ___ this book. It's really good.
items.explanation: A prediction from opinion: **will** + base verb.

items.prompt: The film ___ at 8 p.m., so let's meet at 7:30.
I don't think it ___ tomorrow.
items.explanation: A prediction from opinion: *I don't think* + **will** + base verb.

intro: We use the **present perfect** to talk about experiences in our life up to now, when we don't say exactly when they happened: *I**'ve been** to Japan. She**'s never eaten** sushi. **Have** you **ever ridden** a horse?*
Form: **have / has + past participle**.

sections.h2: How to form the present perfect

rows: I**'ve visited** Paris. He**'s met** a famous actor.
haven't / hasn't + past participle, or have/has + never
I **haven't seen** that film. She**'s never flown**.
Yes, + subject + have/has. / No, + subject + haven't/hasn't.
Yes, I have. / No, she hasn't.

blocks.md: Regular past participles end in -ed (*visited, tried*). Irregular verbs have their own forms (*been, seen, eaten, flown*). See the [irregular verbs list](/blog/grammar/past-simple/).

items: **ever** = at any time in your life. We use it in questions: *Have you **ever** been to Mexico?*
**never** = not at any time. Use it with a positive verb: *I've **never** been to Mexico.* (not *I haven't never been*)

blocks.md: We also use *ever* after superlatives: *It's the best meal I've **ever** had.*
*been to* = went and came back (an experience). *gone to* = went and is still there: *I**'ve been** to London three times. Sam isn't here; he**'s gone** to London.*

Use the present perfect for the experience, with no time: *I**'ve been** to Rome.* When you say **when**, use the past simple: *I **went** there in 2019.* Conversations often start with the present perfect and continue in the past simple: *Have you ever been to Rome? – Yes, I have. I **went** last summer.* More practice: [Present Perfect vs Past Simple](/blog/grammar/present-perfect-vs-past-simple/).
To say how often: *I've seen this film **three times**. How many times **have** you **been** there?*

items.text: I**'ve been** to Canada twice.
**Have** you **ever eaten** octopus?
She**'s never driven** a car.
We **haven't met** your new boyfriend.
He**'s read** all the Harry Potter books.
**Has** your brother **ever lived** abroad?
I**'ve seen** this film three times.
They**'ve never been** on a plane.
It's the most beautiful place I**'ve ever seen**.
Have you ever been to Italy? – Yes, I have. I **went** in 2022.

mistakes.wrong: Have you ever went to London?
mistakes.right: Have you ever been to London?

mistakes.why: Never already makes the sentence negative.

mistakes.wrong: I've been to Paris last year.
mistakes.right: I went to Paris last year.
mistakes.why: With a finished time, use the past simple.

mistakes.wrong: Ever you have been to Japan?
mistakes.right: Have you ever been to Japan?
mistakes.why: Question: Have + subject + ever + past participle.

items.prompt: Have you ever ___ to Australia?
I've never ___ sushi.
___ she ever met a famous person?
We ___ been to that restaurant. Is it good?
My brother ___ in a band.
Have you ever seen a ghost? – No, I ___.
items.explanation: Short answer to a *have* question: *No, I **haven't**.*

items.prompt: I've seen this film ___ times.
It's the best pizza I've ___ eaten.
Have you ever been to Rome? – Yes, I went there ___.
items.explanation: With the past simple, say when: **in 2019**.

items.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I went to Paris last year.
I've been to Paris last year.
I've went to Paris last year.
I go to Paris last year.
items.explanation: *Last year* is a finished time: past simple, **went**.

items.prompt: Sam isn't here. He's ___ to the shops.
items.explanation: He's at the shops now: **gone**. (*Been* = he went and came back.)

items.prompt: How many times ___ you been to London?
She's never ___ a horse.
Have they ever ___ abroad?
___ ever been to a concert?
items.explanation: Present perfect question: **Have you** ever + past participle?

items.prompt: Which sentence talks about an experience?
options: I'm going to climb a mountain.
items.explanation: Life experience, no time given: present perfect, **I've climbed**.

intro: **Could** is the past of *can* for ability. Use it for general abilities in the past: *I **could** swim when I was five.*
The negative is **couldn't**: *I **couldn't** sleep last night.*

sections.h2: How to form could and couldn't

rows: She **could** play the violin at six.
**Could** you read when you were four?
Yes, + subject + could. / No, + subject + couldn't.
Yes, I could. / No, I couldn't.

blocks.md: Like *can*, *could* is the same for every person, with no -s and no *to*: *He **could** run fast.* (not *He coulds* or *could to run*)

For a **general** ability in the past, use *could*: *My grandfather **could** speak five languages.* For **one specific success** in a particular situation, use **was / were able to** or **managed to**, not *could*: *The fire was big, but everyone **was able to** escape.* (not *could escape*)
In the **negative**, *couldn't* is fine for both: *I **couldn't** find my keys this morning.*
With verbs of the senses (*see, hear, smell, taste, feel*) and with *understand* and *remember*, *could* is fine for a specific situation: *I **could** see the mountains from my window.*

items.text: I **could** read before I started school.
She **couldn't** speak English when she arrived in Canada.
**Could** you swim when you were a child?
We **couldn't** go to the beach because it was raining.
My dad **could** run very fast when he was young.
I **couldn't** find a parking space.
After two hours, we **managed to** fix the car.
The test was hard, but I **was able to** answer all the questions.
I **could** hear music from the next room.
They **couldn't** understand the instructions.

mistakes.wrong: I could to swim when I was six.
mistakes.right: I could swim when I was six.

mistakes.wrong: Last night I could finish my essay on time.
mistakes.right: Last night I managed to finish my essay on time.
mistakes.why: One specific success: managed to or was able to.

mistakes.wrong: Could you to ride a bike?
When I was five, I can swim.
mistakes.right: When I was five, I could swim.

items.prompt: When I was four, I ___ read.
items.explanation: General ability in the past: **could** + base verb.

items.prompt: My grandmother ___ play the piano beautifully.
I ___ sleep last night because of the noise.
___ you speak English when you were a child?
items.explanation: Past ability question: **Could** + subject + base verb?

items.prompt: The exam was difficult, but I ___ pass it.
items.explanation: One specific success: **was able to**, not *could*.

items.prompt: Could you ride a bike when you were five? – Yes, I ___.
She ___ swim when she was three.
We ___ go to the park because it was raining.
items.explanation: Not possible in the past: **couldn't**. (*Weren't able* needs *to*.)

items.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I didn't could find my keys.
I couldn't to find my keys.
I not could find my keys.

items.prompt: I tried for hours, and finally I ___ open the box.
items.explanation: One success after trying hard: **managed to**.

items.prompt: I ___ hear the birds from my bedroom window this morning.
items.explanation: With verbs of the senses, **could** is fine for one situation.

items.prompt: When he was young, he ___ run 10 kilometres easily.
Which sentence is about one specific success in the past?
options: I could swim when I was six.
She could speak French as a child.
We were able to catch the last train.
items.explanation: **Were able to** describes one success in a particular situation.

items.prompt: ___ you understand the film? It was in Italian.
items.explanation: Past ability question: **Could** you understand…? (*understand* works with could)

items.prompt: They ___ understand the teacher because she spoke too fast.
When I was a teenager, I ___ stay out late. My parents were very strict.
items.explanation: Not allowed / not possible in the past: **couldn't**.

intro: We use **must** and **have to** for obligation (something is necessary), and **should** for advice (something is a good idea).
*You **must** wear a seatbelt. I **have to** work on Saturday. You **should** see a doctor.*

rows: I **have to** go / she **has to** go
**Do** I **have to** go? **Does** she **have to** go?

blocks.md: *Must* and *should* never take *to* or *-s*: *She **must** go* (not *musts* or *must to*). *Have to* changes like a normal verb: *has to, had to, will have to*.
These look similar but mean very different things:

items: ***mustn't*** = it's not allowed, don't do it: *You **mustn't** smoke here.*
***don't have to*** = it's not necessary, but you can if you want: *You **don't have to** pay. It's free.*

blocks.md: In the present positive, both are often possible. *Must* is common in rules and signs, and when the speaker decides: *Passengers **must** show their tickets. I **must** call Mum tonight.* *Have to* is common when the obligation comes from outside (a job, a law): *I **have to** wear a uniform at work.*
For the past and future, use *have to*: *Yesterday I **had to** work late. Next year I'll **have to** take the exam again.*

She **has to** get up at 5 for work.

You **should** try this cake. It's delicious.

**Should** I call her?

topics.h1: Much, Many, A Lot Of, A Few, A Little
intro: We use these words to talk about **quantity**. The choice depends on the noun: **countable** nouns (*apples, friends*) or **uncountable** nouns (*milk, time, money*).
*How **many** apples? How **much** milk? I've got **a few** friends and **a little** time.*

blocks.md: In everyday English, *much* and *many* are most common in **negatives and questions**: *I don't have **much** time. Are there **many** people?* In positive sentences, *a lot of* sounds more natural: *I have **a lot of** time.*

sections.h2: A few or few? A little or little?

blocks.md: ***A few / a little*** = some, a small amount (positive): *I have **a few** friends here, so I'm happy.*
***Few / little*** = not many, not much, almost none (negative): *Very **few** people came, so we cancelled the meeting. We have **little** time. Hurry!*

intro: When one verb follows another, the second verb is either **to + verb** or **verb-ing**. It depends on the **first** verb: *I **want to go**. I **enjoy going**.*
There is no simple rule, so learn the most common verbs in each group.

blocks.md: *want, need, would like, decide, hope, plan, learn, promise, agree, offer, refuse, expect, manage, can't afford*

items.text: I **want to learn** Italian.
We **decided to stay** at home.
She **promised to call** me.

blocks.md: *enjoy, finish, don't mind, can't stand, practise, miss, keep, avoid, suggest, imagine, feel like*

items.text: I **enjoy cooking** for my friends.
Have you **finished eating**?
He **keeps asking** the same question.

blocks.md: After *like, love, hate, start, begin* and *continue*, both forms are possible with the same meaning: *It started **to rain** / It started **raining**. I love **to swim** / I love **swimming**.*
But after *would like, would love* and *would prefer*, use **to**: *I'd love **to come**.* (not *I'd love coming*)
A few verbs, like *remember, stop* and *try*, change their meaning with -ing or to. See [Gerund or Infinitive?](/blog/grammar/gerund-or-infinitive/).

items: Negative: put **not** before *to* or *-ing*: *I decided **not to go**. I enjoy **not having** to get up early.*
After a preposition, always use **-ing**: *I'm good **at cooking**. Thanks **for helping**. She's interested **in learning** Spanish.*

topics.h1: Infinitive of Purpose (I went out to buy milk)
intro: We use **to + verb** to say **why** we do something: *I went to the shop **to buy** some milk.* (Why did I go? To buy milk.)
This is called the **infinitive of purpose**.

blocks.md: *She's learning English **to get** a better job. I called him **to say** thank you.*
It's also a short answer to *Why?*: *Why are you saving money? – **To buy** a car.*
Don't use *for* before a verb: *I came here **to see** you* (not *for see* or *for to see*).

rows: I went out **to get** some food.

sections.h2: In order to and so as to

blocks.md: *In order to* and *so as to* mean the same as *to*, but they're more formal: *We left early **in order to** avoid the traffic.*
For a negative purpose, use ***in order not to*** or ***so as not to***: *Speak quietly **so as not to** wake the baby.* (not *to not wake* in formal English)

This bag is **for carrying** my laptop.
They studied hard **in order to** pass the exam.
Close the window **so as not to** let the cold in.
I'm going to the station **to meet** my aunt.

intro: **Adverbs of manner** tell us **how** someone does something: *She speaks **quietly**. He drives **carefully**. They play **well**.*
An **adjective** describes a noun (*a careful driver*); an **adverb** describes a verb (*he drives carefully*).

rows: quick → quickly, bad → badly, careful → carefully
happy → happily, easy → easily, angry → angrily
terrible → terribly, gentle → gently, comfortable → comfortably

blocks.md: *Hardly* and *lately* are different words: *hardly* = almost not (*I can **hardly** hear you*), *lately* = recently (*I haven't seen him **lately***).
Put the adverb **after the verb**, or **after the object** if there is one: *She speaks **slowly**. She speaks English **slowly**.* (not *She speaks slowly English*)
After *be, look, feel, seem, sound, taste, smell*, use an **adjective**, because it describes the subject: *You **look happy**. This soup **tastes delicious**. That **sounds great**.*

intro: The **zero conditional** talks about things that are **always true**: *If you heat ice, it **melts**.*
The **first conditional** talks about a **real possibility in the future**: *If it **rains** tomorrow, we**'ll stay** at home.*

rows: If you **mix** red and white, you **get** pink.
**will** / can / might + verb, or an imperative
If you **study**, you**'ll pass**. If you're cold, **close** the window.

blocks.md: Don't use *will* in the *if* clause: *If it **rains**…* (not *If it will rain*).
The clauses can go in either order. Use a comma when *if* comes first: *If you hurry, you'll catch the bus. / You'll catch the bus if you hurry.*

items: ***if*** = maybe it will happen: *If I see Tom, I'll tell him.*
***when*** = I'm sure it will happen: *I'll call you **when** I get home.* (present tense after *when* too)
***unless*** = if not: *You can't come in **unless** you have a ticket.* (= if you don't have a ticket)

intro: Many adjectives are followed by a **fixed preposition**: *I'm **good at** maths. She's **interested in** art. He's **married to** a doctor.*
The preposition is often different from your language, so learn each adjective together with its preposition.

blocks.md: You'll also hear *different to* (British English) and *different than* (American English). *Different from* is correct everywhere.
After the preposition, use a noun, a pronoun or a verb**-ing**: *I'm good at **languages**. I'm proud of **you**. I'm tired of **waiting**.* (not *tired of wait*)

intro: **Possessive pronouns** (*mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs*) replace a possessive adjective + noun: *This is **my** bag. → This bag is **mine**.*
We use them so we don't repeat the noun: *Your car is red, and **mine** is blue.*

blocks.md: Possessive pronouns never have an apostrophe: *yours, hers, ours, theirs* (not *your's, her's*). And don't use *the* before them: *It's **mine*** (not *the mine*).
*Its* is almost never used as a possessive pronoun. Say *its* + noun: *The dog wants **its** dinner.*
Use **whose** to ask who something belongs to. Answer with a possessive pronoun or 's: ***Whose** keys are these? – They're **mine**. / They're **Tom's**.*
We say ***a friend of mine***, *a cousin of hers*, *a colleague of ours* = one of my friends, one of her cousins. (not *a friend of me*)

intro: Many adjectives have two forms. The **-ed** adjective describes how a **person feels**. The **-ing** adjective describes the **thing (or person) that causes** the feeling.

intro: Use **no article** to talk about things **in general**: ***Dogs** are friendly. **Coffee** is expensive.*
Use **the** for **specific** things that the listener knows: ***The dogs** next door are friendly. **The coffee** in this café is expensive.*

blocks.md: With plural and uncountable nouns used in general, don't use *the*: *I love **music**. **Children** need **sleep**. **Life** is short.* (not *The life is short*)
